children: Nvidia Corp.'s investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy has raised a series of once-unthinkable questions, including whether the man at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom could be at risk of losing his job.

Nvidia shares slid as much as 8.8% on Monday after Huang disclosed the romantic relationship in a memo to employees, at one point wiping out nearly $400 billion in market value. The company's board is assembling a committee of independent directors who will work with external legal counsel to investigate the matter.

The revelation has left investors weighing a range of possibilities that could affect not just Huang and Nvidia, but the entire AI industry. Nvidia, the leading maker of AI chips, has used its financial strength to back dozens of major players, from frontier labs such as OpenAI to cloud computing companies such as CoreWeave Inc. Huang has also been among the most vocal advocates of AI, from Washington to Wall Street.

“It brings the stewardship of one of America's most important companies, and the architect of the US AI trajectory, under debate, as well as calling judgment into account,” Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said in a note.
Huang had previously said there was nothing inappropriate about his relationship with the woman, who worked for a Singapore-based customer.
“I was unfaithful to my wife,” Huang, 63, said in the memo. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

It was a humbling moment for one of Silicon Valley's biggest celebrities. Huang has criss-crossed the globe promoting AI computing, drawing crowds of fans swept up in “Jensanity”. His relentless public appearances, featuring science lectures, dad jokes and his signature leather jackets, have turned him into AI's biggest cheerleader.

The incident threatens to further unsettle an AI market already shaken by concerns about a slowdown in data centre spending. Nvidia makes chips that are crucial to AI computing equipment and is one of the world's most valuable companies. Turmoil within the company risks reverberating across the broader industry.

Nvidia has emerged as a key source of financing for AI infrastructure. Huang has worked with some of Wall Street's biggest firms on a $500 billion effort to help companies rapidly build out their equipment. He has also channelled money into strengthening the AI supply chain and supporting fledgling customers.
“Jensen is a very unique CEO,” said Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group. “There is no known succession plan. There are no leaders in his company that would be the clear next to step up.”

Nvidia's board said in a statement that it has confidence in Huang and has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”. However, it promised that the inquiry “will examine all available information”.
US President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday, calling him a “fine person” and saying he should remain CEO.
“I have not spoken to him about it,” Trump told reporters. “I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on.”
Last week, key House Republicans requested a briefing with Huang to discuss his dealings with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le.
The probe follows a series of reports that Nvidia's leader was targeted by former Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, whom the US government suspects was recruited by a Chinese spy agency.

The CEO had previously described his relationship with the woman, who is no longer with Megaspeed, as “normal”. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun had called the characterisation of the woman as a Chinese agent an unsubstantiated “smear against China”.

The board investigation will address reports that the chip magnate “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”, the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.”
In his memo, Huang said he would support the investigation. “I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security,” he said.

Nvidia's co-founder, known for his hands-on and tireless management style, built the graphics card maker into arguably the world's most important technology company. Nvidia's highly prized accelerator chips are used to develop and run AI models. The company has also expanded into related areas, including computers, networking and software.

Huang's interactions with fans have occasionally grown raucous. During one autograph session, a young woman asked him to sign her chest. After asking her if she was sure, he signed her brassiere while looking off to one side and asking, “Is that a good idea?”

Huang has also been a leading voice in trying to calm fears about AI technology slipping out of human control. He has dismissed calls for AI labs to slow down their work to ensure it does not threaten humanity, even as industry leaders such as Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have endorsed such an idea. He has also argued that new regulations are unnecessary.
What Bloomberg Economics says

Congress will soon return and begin negotiations over the final form of the fiscal 2027 defence bill. Senate National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA) negotiations already include proposals on chip-location verification, remote access and advanced AI chip exports. Nvidia and AMD have been lobbying the White House and Commerce Department to press lawmakers to remove or narrow these provisions.
The affair could further weaken Nvidia's position as Democrats take control of committees in January after winning both chambers, bringing greater scrutiny of its chip sales to China.
Michael Deng, geoeconomics technology analyst

The Santa Clara, California-based company has no public succession plan, and there is no obvious heir apparent to Huang. He has repeatedly said he wants to continue in his role for decades and has created an informal organisational structure that eschews a conventional hierarchy. Instead, his direct reports are tasked with rapidly implementing his decisions.

Huang has said this system gives his company the flexibility to respond to rapid technological changes and remain agile. However, it has also created a situation in which there is no ready replacement to take over Huang's demanding schedule.

The latest revelations “highlight the considerable key man risk that Nvidia faces,” Rasgon said. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia, clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction, and (with supposedly 60 direct reports) pulls most of the company's strings himself.”

Concerns that sensitive information might leak through Nvidia's contacts with China have fuelled calls for investigations and greater scrutiny of Huang and the company, adding to pressure in what has already been a difficult geopolitical balancing act.

While Nvidia is allowed to ship a limited range of products to China under a licensing programme granted by the Trump administration, Beijing has restricted imports of the chips. The impasse continues to curb the chipmaker's sales in the world's second-largest economy.

Huang has long sought to sell more of Nvidia's AI processors in China, the world's largest chip market. He has argued that Nvidia and its peers should be allowed to serve the region to keep their products central to AI development. Closing off the market, he has said, risks turning China into a more powerful and independent force in artificial intelligence.
Investors have poured money into Nvidia, which is due to report earnings later this month, betting that it will continue to be the main beneficiary of runaway spending on AI infrastructure.

The company reached a record market capitalisation of nearly $5.8 trillion in October. That figure has since slipped below $5 trillion, weighed down by concerns about the sustainability of the AI infrastructure build-out.
Megaspeed, based in Singapore, has been accused of breaking US export restrictions and smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
Huang had previously told Bloomberg that his contacts with Megaspeed employees were typical of the business relationships he maintains with Chinese customers and executives.

title: Nvidia probe into CEO affair raises thorny questions for AI
